column2: All knowledge will shine for you, blameless one, and attachment of your intellect will never arise anywhere.
Your mind, Bhishma, will always abide in sattva, free of rajas and tamas, like the moon freed from clouds.
Whatever is joined to dharma or to wealth that you consider, in that your intellect will be supreme.
And this fourfold host of beings, tiger among kings, you will behold, resorting to divine sight, of immeasurable valour.
Joined to the eye of knowledge, Bhishma, you will see in truth the fourfold net of creatures, like fish in clear water."
[Vaishampayana said:] Then all the great sages with Vyasa honoured Krishna with words joined to Rik, Yajus and Saman.
Then a divine rain of flowers of all seasons fell from the sky where Vrishni, Gangeya and the Pandava were.
Divine instruments played and hosts of Apsarases sang; nothing hostile or unpleasant was seen there.
A pure, pleasant, auspicious wind blew, bearing all scents; the quarter was calm and beasts and birds called peacefully.
Then after a moment the revered thousand-rayed sun was seen in the west, as if burning a forest in a solitary place.
Then all the great sages rose and took leave of Janardana, Bhishma and King Yudhishthira.
Then Keshava, the Pandava, Satyaki, Sanjaya and Kripa Sharadvata bowed.
Then, duly honoured by them, devoted to dharma, saying "We shall meet tomorrow," they went hastily as they wished.
Likewise, taking leave of Gangeya, Keshava and the Pandavas, circumambulating him, mounted their bright chariots.
Then with chariots with golden-tusked poles, with rutting elephants like mountains, with swift horses like Garuda, and foot-soldiers with bows and other weapons in hand,
that army went in front of the chariots, and just so behind, exceedingly swift, in front and behind, like a great river, like the Narmada reaching the Riksha mountain.
Then in front the revered moon rose, gladdening that army, restoring the herbs, whose sap the sun had drunk, to their own quality again.
Then entering the city, radiant like the city of the gods, the bulls of the Yadus and Pandavas went to their fine dwellings, weary, like lions to caves.
Taking the path of meditation, Madhava surveyed all knowledge and then meditated on the eternal Brahma.
Then those who knew the Vedas and Puranas, trained, red-throated, praised Vishvakarman, Vasudeva, the Prajapati.
Reciters struck their hands to mark time and singers sang; conches, anakas and mridangas were played by thousands.
The sound of lutes, tabors and flutes, exceedingly lovely, was heard from his house like spreading laughter.
Likewise in King Yudhishthira's house sweet auspicious voices joined to song and music rose.
Then Dasharha, Achyuta, mighty-armed, rose, bathed, with joined palms, recited the secret prayer, and stood resorting to the fires.
Then Madhava had a thousand Brahmanas who knew the four Vedas pronounce blessings, giving each a thousand cows.
Having performed the auspicious touching and looked at himself in a spotless mirror, Krishna then said to Satyaki:

The best of chariots of the wise Vasudeva is yoked, O king; Janardana will go to the son of Ganga.
mahabharata:12:53.13	Krishna awaits you, king of dharma, greatly radiant; whatever next is to be done here, you should do it.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Have my best chariot yoked, Phalguna, incomparably radiant; we shall not go with soldiers; we shall go alone.
Bhishma, best of the upholders of dharma, is not to be troubled by me; so let the vanguard turn back, Dhananjaya.
From today Gangeya will tell the supreme secret; therefore I do not want the company of ordinary people, son of Kunti."
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing those words, Dhananjaya son of Kunti told him that the best chariot was yoked, bull among men.
Then King Yudhishthira, the twins and Bhima and Arjuna went to Krishna's dwelling like all the elements.
As the great-souled Pandavas arrived, wise Krishna with Shaineya (Satyaki) also mounted the chariot.
Seated in their chariots, having agreed and asked about the night's comfort, those great chariot-warriors set out in chariots rumbling like clouds.
Daruka urged Vasudeva's horses Meghapushpa, Balaha, Sainya and Sugriva.
Urged by Daruka, Vasudeva's horses went then, O king, scoring the ground with the tips of their hooves.
As if devouring the sky, swift and mighty, they descended to Kurukshetra, the field of all dharma.
Then they went where Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows, the lord, with Brahmin-sages, as Brahma with hosts of gods.
Then Govinda descended from the chariot, with Yudhishthira, Bhima, the wielder of Gandiva, the twins and Satyaki, and with right hands raised they honoured the sages.
Surrounded by them, like the moon by stars, the king came to Gangeya as Vasava to Brahma.
He saw him lying on his bed of arrows like a fallen sun, the mighty-armed one, coming near with awe from fear.

When Bhishma, delight of Shantanu, lay on his hero's bed, and the Pandavas had attended the tiger among men, Gangeya,
mahabharata:12:54.3	what talks took place at that meeting of heroes, when all the armies were slain? Tell me that, great sage.
[Vaishampayana said:] "When Bhishma, bearer of the Kuru burden, lay on his bed of arrows, sages and perfected ones led by Narada came, O king.
And the remaining kings, led by Yudhishthira, and Dhritarashtra, Krishna, Bhima, Arjuna and the twins.
Those great souls, approaching, mourned the grandsire of the Bharatas, Gangeya, like a fallen sun.
After reflecting a moment, Narada, godlike to see, said to all the Pandavas and remaining kings:

It is the time; let Bhishma be questioned. Gangeya is setting like the sun, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:54.9	He wishes to give up his life; all of you go to him and ask; for he knows fully the various dharmas of the four classes.
Thus told by Narada, the kings went to Bhishma, but could not ask and looked at one another.
Then Yudhishthira, son of Pandu, said to Hrishikesha: "None but you, son of Devaki, is able to question the grandsire.
Speak first, invincible Madhusudana, for you are the best of us all, dear one, knower of all dharma."
Thus told by the Pandava, the revered Keshava, Achyuta, approached the invincible one and spoke.

Has the night passed pleasantly for you, best of kings? Is your intellect of clear marks and present?
mahabharata:12:54.16	Do all the knowledges shine for you, blameless one? Your heart is not wearied nor your mind troubled?

Burning, delusion, weariness, fatigue, languor and pain have by your grace, Govinda, at once left me, blameless one.
mahabharata:12:54.18	Whatever has been, will be and is, greatly radiant one, I see it all as a fruit in the palm of the hand.
mahabharata:12:54.19	The dharmas declared in the Vedas and those placed in the Vedanta, I see them all by your boon, Achyuta.
mahabharata:12:54.20	And the dharma declared by the good is in my heart; I know the dharma of lands, castes and families, Janardana.
mahabharata:12:54.21	What is the meaning in the dharmas of the four stages of life is in my heart, and I understand all the duties of kings, Keshava.
mahabharata:12:54.22	Wherever there is to be speech I shall speak, Janardana; for by your grace a bright wisdom has entered my mind.
mahabharata:12:54.23	I have become as if young, strengthened by meditation on you; by your grace, Janardana, I am able to speak what is best.
mahabharata:12:54.24	Why, revered one, did you yourself not tell the Pandava what is best? What do you wish to say here? Say it quickly, Madhava.

Know me, Kaurava, as the root of fame and of the good; all states, existent and non-existent, come from me.
mahabharata:12:54.26	When the cool-rayed one is called the moon, who in the world will marvel? So who will marvel at me when I am full of fame?
mahabharata:12:54.27	But I wish more fame to be placed on you, greatly radiant one; therefore my wide intelligence is directed to you, Bhishma.
mahabharata:12:54.28	As long as the earth, lord of the earth, shall stand firm, so long your imperishable fame will move through the worlds.
mahabharata:12:54.29	And what you, Bhishma, will say to the Pandava who asks will stand on earth like the Vedic teachings.
mahabharata:12:54.30	And he who joins himself to this standard by himself will gain the fruit of all merits and enjoy it after death.
mahabharata:12:54.31	For this reason, Bhishma, I gave you a divine mind in this great welfare: that your fame might spread more.
mahabharata:12:54.32	It is certain that as long as a man's fame spreads on earth in the world, so long he has an imperishable place.
mahabharata:12:54.33	The remaining kings, O king, sit around you, wishing to ask about dharmas; speak to them, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:54.34	You are old in years, endowed with learning and conduct, skilled in the duties of kings, earlier and later.
mahabharata:12:54.35	From birth no one has seen any fault in you; all kings know you as the knower of dharma.
mahabharata:12:54.36	Speak to them, O king, the supreme policy, as a father to sons; for sages and gods are always served by you.
mahabharata:12:54.37	Therefore it must be said here by you; I see it entirely: the wise say that when asked by good men wishing to hear dharma it must be said again.
mahabharata:12:54.38	It must be said by the learned; so say the wise. For one who gives no answer, lord, there is a painful fault.
mahabharata:12:54.39	Therefore, bull of the Bharatas, learned one, tell the eternal dharmas when asked by sons and grandsons who wish to know.

By your grace, Govinda, you are the eternal soul of beings; but let King Yudhishthira ask me about dharmas.
mahabharata:12:55.3	Thus I shall be pleased and shall speak dharmas, blameless one; let the Pandava ask me in whom all royal sages dwell.
mahabharata:12:55.4	Let the Pandava ask me, whom no one among all the renowned dharma-practising Kurus equals.
mahabharata:12:55.5	In whom are steadfastness, restraint, celibacy and forbearance, ever dharma, vigour and splendour—let that Pandava ask me.
mahabharata:12:55.6	Truth, giving, austerity, purity, peace, skill and calm: in whom are all these—let that Pandava ask me.
mahabharata:12:55.7	He who would not do unrighteousness out of desire, anger, fear or for gain, the righteous-souled—let that Pandava ask me.
mahabharata:12:55.8	He who honours relatives, guests, servants, dependants and those close, treating them well—let that Pandava ask me.
mahabharata:12:55.9	Ever truthful, ever forbearing, ever devoted to knowledge, fond of guests, who always gives to the good—let that Pandava ask me.

The righteous Yudhishthira, full of shame, afraid of a curse, does not approach you.
mahabharata:12:55.12	Having made slaughter of the world, the lord of the world, lord of men, afraid of a curse, does not approach you.
mahabharata:12:55.13	Having slain with arrows the worthy of honour, the respected, the devoted, teachers, kinsmen and relatives, he does not approach you.

As dharma for Brahmanas is giving, study and austerity, so for kshatriyas, Krishna, it is falling in battle.
mahabharata:12:55.15	Fathers, grandfathers, sons, teachers, kinsmen and relatives acting falsely—one who slays them in battle acts by dharma.
mahabharata:12:55.16	A kshatriya who in battle slays the agreement-breakers, the greedy, even teachers, Keshava, the sinners, is a knower of dharma.
mahabharata:12:55.17	A kshatriya, when challenged, should always fight in battle; for Manu said that battle is lawful, leads to heaven and is worldly good.
Thus addressed by Bhishma, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, approached humbly and stood in his sight.
Then Bhishma took his feet and welcomed him, smelled his head and said, "Sit."
Then Gangeya, the bull among all bowmen, said to him, "Ask me, dear one, confidently; do not be afraid, best of the Kurus."

Those who know dharma know that kingship is the supreme dharma, and I consider it a great burden; tell me of it, king.
mahabharata:12:56.3	Tell, grandsire, especially the duties of kings, for the duties of kings are the refuge of the whole living world.
mahabharata:12:56.4	The triple aim is bound up here in the duties of kings, Kaurava, and the whole of the dharma of liberation is clearly contained here.
mahabharata:12:56.5	As the reins of a horse and the goad of an elephant, so, lord of men, is dharma for the world, and so is control said to be.
mahabharata:12:56.6	If this dharma, served by royal sages, were bewildered here, the order of the world would not stand and everything would be thrown into confusion.
mahabharata:12:56.7	As the rising sun destroys the darkness of the asuras, so the duties of kings, when considered, drive out an evil course.
mahabharata:12:56.8	First, grandsire, tell the essence of the duties of kings, best of the Bharatas, for you are the best of the wise.
mahabharata:12:56.9	You are the source and the supreme authority for all of us, scorcher of foes; Vasudeva regards you as supreme in wisdom.

At the very beginning, best of the Kurus, a king should act duly toward gods and Brahmanas, wishing to please.
mahabharata:12:56.13	Having honoured the deities and Brahmanas, delight of the Kurus, he becomes quit of his debt to dharma and is honoured by the world.
mahabharata:12:56.14	Always strive in effort, son, Yudhishthira; for without effort fate does not accomplish kings' aims.
mahabharata:12:56.15	Fate and effort are a pair held in common; but I consider human effort supreme, and fate is said to be determined.
mahabharata:12:56.16	When an undertaking fails, do not be distressed; discipline is attainable, dear one; this is the highest policy of kings.
mahabharata:12:56.17	For kings there is no cause of success but truth; a king devoted to truth rejoices both here and hereafter.
mahabharata:12:56.18	Even for sages, king, truth is the supreme wealth; and for a king there is no other cause of trust than truth.
mahabharata:12:56.19	A king who is virtuous, of good conduct, self-controlled, gentle, righteous, with senses subdued, far-sighted and of wide aims never falls from fortune.
mahabharata:12:56.20	Resort to uprightness in all matters, delight of the Kurus, with repeated consideration of policy and with concealment by the triple learning.
mahabharata:12:56.21	A gentle king is always despised by all; the world is troubled by a harsh one; therefore practise both.
mahabharata:12:56.22	Brahmanas should always be exempt from punishment by you, best of givers; Brahmanas are the greatest being in the world, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:56.23	Two verses sung by the great-souled Manu you should take to heart in your dharmas, O king.
mahabharata:12:56.24	From water came fire, from Brahmana the kshatriya, from stone iron; their pervading energy is quenched in their own wombs.
mahabharata:12:56.25	When iron strikes stone, fire enters water, and a kshatriya hates a Brahmana, the three sink.
mahabharata:12:56.26	Knowing this, great king, those twice-born are to be honoured; the best of the twice-born, tranquil, bear earthly Brahma.
mahabharata:12:56.27	Thus, tiger among men, those who would destroy the order of the world are always to be restrained by force of arms.
mahabharata:12:56.28	Two verses were sung long ago by the great sage Ushanas, dear one; hear them, wise king, with a single mind.
mahabharata:12:56.29	A king, looking to dharma, should restrain by his own dharma even one who comes against him with weapon raised, though learned in the Vedanta, in battle.
mahabharata:12:56.30	He who protects dharma when it is being destroyed is a knower of dharma; he is not a slayer of an embryo; anger meets anger.
mahabharata:12:56.31	Thus, best of men, the twice-born are to be protected; for their offences one should dismiss them to the border of the land.
mahabharata:12:56.32	Even if they are accused, lord of men, one should show them pity: for a slayer of a Brahmana, a defiler of a teacher's bed, a slayer of an embryo, and an enemy of the king.
mahabharata:12:56.33	Dismissal to the border of the land is prescribed for a Brahmana; there is never bodily harm for them.
mahabharata:12:56.34	Let men be dear to you always, best of men; for there is no treasury greater for kings than the gathering of men.
mahabharata:12:56.35	Of the six forts, great king, which are decided by the scriptures, in all these they consider the human fort the hardest to cross.
mahabharata:12:56.36	Therefore the wise should always show kindness to the four classes; a righteous, truthful king pleases the subjects.
mahabharata:12:56.37	You should not always be forbearing, best of men; a gentle king is unrighteous, like a forbearing elephant.
mahabharata:12:56.38	Verses were laid down of old in the science of Brihaspati on this matter, great king; hear them as I tell them.
mahabharata:12:56.39	A low man scorns a ever-forbearing king, as an elephant-driver wishes to climb onto an elephant's head.
mahabharata:12:56.40	Therefore a king should be neither always gentle nor always harsh, like the sun in spring, glorious, neither cold nor hot.
mahabharata:12:56.41	By perception, inference and analogy and instruction, your own and others should always be tested, great king.
mahabharata:12:56.42	Give up all vices, giver of abundant fees; and not engage in them; avoid attachment.
mahabharata:12:56.43	A man of vice is ever despised in the world; a king who is excessively hateful troubles the world.
mahabharata:12:56.44	A king should always be like a pregnant woman who shares dharma; hear the reason why it is so said, great king.
mahabharata:12:56.45	As a pregnant woman, abandoning her own pleasure that follows her mind, bestows what is good for the embryo, so surely a king too.
mahabharata:12:56.46	Should act, best of the Kurus, ever following dharma, abandoning his own pleasure and doing whatever would be of benefit to the world.
mahabharata:12:56.47	You must never give up your steadfastness, Pandava; the command of a steady one who wields the rod openly is not obstructed.
mahabharata:12:56.48	You should not jest always with your servants, best of speakers, tiger among kings; hear the fault in that from me.
mahabharata:12:56.49	Dependants, out of familiarity, scorn their master, they do not stay in their place and they transgress his command.
mahabharata:12:56.50	Sent on errands they hesitate and pry into secrets; they ask for what should not be asked and bring food not to be eaten.
mahabharata:12:56.51	They get angry and blaze up, and take a fearsome seat, and by bribes and deceits they hinder his affairs.
mahabharata:12:56.52	They make his realm decayed by imitations, they attach themselves to women with their eyes, and take equal dress.
mahabharata:12:56.53	They pass wind and spit in his presence and, shameless, tiger among men, speak his words.
mahabharata:12:56.54	They mount a horse, elephant or chariot approved by the king without regard, when the king is gentle and merry.
mahabharata:12:56.55	This is hard for you, king; this is badly done by you," thus, calling themselves friends, they say in the assembly.
When he is angry they laugh, and when honoured they do not rejoice; they are ever quarrelsome with one another for some cause.
They reveal his counsel and expose his misdeed, and play at carrying out his command with contempt, enjoying ornaments, food, bathing and unguents.
Scorning him, tiger among men, they sit at ease and listen to him; they revile their own offices and give them up, Bharata.
They are not content with their pay and take what is due to the king; they wish to play with him like a bird on a string; and they say in the world, "The king is to be led by us."
These and other faults arise, Yudhishthira, in a king who is gentle and merry."
The revered Ushanas spoke a verse on this, lord of men; hear it from me as I recite it, with a single mind, O king.
The earth swallows these two, as a serpent lying in its hole: a king who does not resist and a Brahmana who does not travel.
Take this to heart, tiger among men: make peace with those fit for peace, and oppose those to be opposed.
Whoever acts contrarily in your realm of seven parts, whether teacher or friend, is to be struck down.
This ancient verse was sung by King Marutta, in the matter of kingship, long ago, approved by Brihaspati:
Even a teacher who is proud, ignorant of what should and should not be done, and gone on a wrong path is to be abandoned.
The wise King Sagara, son of Bahu, abandoned his eldest son Asamanja, wishing the welfare of the city people.
Asamanja once drowned children of the city in the Sarayu, O king, and was therefore scolded by his father and banished.
The sage Uddalaka too abandoned his dear son, the great ascetic Shvetaketu, who served Brahmanas falsely.
Pleasing the people is the eternal dharma of kings here, with protection of truth and uprightness in dealings.
He should not harm others' property and should have what is due given in time; a king valiant, truthful and forbearing does not leave the path.
Keeping counsel secret, having conquered anger, firm in the meaning of the scriptures, ever devoted to dharma, wealth, desire and liberation,
a king deserves to be one whose weak points are covered by the triple learning; there is nothing greater for kings than concealment of fault.
The dharmas of the four classes must be protected by the king, for the protection against mixture of dharmas is the eternal dharma of kings.
A king should neither trust nor distrust too much, and should always consider with his intellect the merits and faults of the six measures of policy.
A king who looks for the weak points of his enemy is always praised, as is one who knows the aims of the triple aim and has appropriate spies and devices."
[Death said:] "We two are helpless, under Time's sway, and doers of what is fated; we are not to be blamed, if you consider rightly."
[Vyasa said:] "If you wish to hear, Partha, hear of King Karandhama, at what time that mighty and rich king lived.
Then, in the fifteenth year, King Dhritarashtra became disgusted, pained by Bhima's arrow-like words.
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, overcome by Time, did not see Uddhava go, covering heaven and earth with his splendour.
[Yudhishthira said:] "'I could burn my enemies in a single day,' said Arjuna, and he did not do it; this boaster fell for that."
Thus many wretched words of the afflicted he heard in that place, on every side, from those who spoke, O king.
